current_episode.title: How To Be An Effective Mentor Who Builds The Next Generation Of Leaders - Winning with Eric Dillon, President of General Bank of Canada

guest.bio_context: Eric Dillon is a banker with 30 years of experience in the finance industry, primarily in Alberta. He has held leadership roles managing teams as large as 2000 people and is deeply passionate about advancing gender diversity in banking and finance while building the next generation of leaders through structured mentoring relationships.

context.real_quote: The primary job of leaders is to build more leaders. Like before the business success, before celebrate the results for the year or whatever the case may be, the primary job of leaders is to actually build more leaders.

pending_qa.q: How should leaders approach candid feedback and transparency in mentoring relationships?
pending_qa.r: Dillon was more hesitant about directness in his early mentoring years but became increasingly courageous and unapologetic about it. He now matter-of-factly tells mentees to own their development, be transparent with their leaders about mentoring relationships, and discuss why, where, how, and with whom they are pursuing development. This transparency can sometimes ignite interest from the mentee's direct leader and create a more productive relationship overall.

pending_qa.q: How has the nature of business capital changed in financial services, and what does this mean for leadership?
pending_qa.r: Historically, capital in banking meant money locked in vaults to build plants and create economic goodwill. Today, Dillon argues, organizational capital is largely human potential—and employees go home every night. Leaders must create environments where people choose to return to work, invest in their futures, and set them up for success. In finance, this shift is more pronounced than ever, as the industry increasingly depends on knowledge workers rather than repeatable tasks.

pending_qa.q: What role might artificial intelligence play in the future of leadership and human capability?
pending_qa.r: While some argue AI will diminish the importance of people, Dillon believes it will accelerate the need for human judgment and leadership. As AI and tools handle easier repeatable tasks, the ability to exercise judgment, have courageous conversations, and harvest diversity become even more critical—capabilities that tools cannot yet replicate.

pending_qa.q: How should organizations handle talented employees who seek opportunities the company cannot provide?
pending_qa.r: Rather than holding employees back, Dillon advocates setting them up for success and allowing them to move on if the organization lacks the opportunity they are passionate about. Good things happen to good people, and employees who leave well-equipped may return three years later as much more capable and better-equipped professionals for challenges the organization faces at that time.
